1Introduction

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Flag: draft prose, ≈0.6 page. The contribution list is the part to keep verbatim; the opening can be reworded to taste.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics discretises a fluid by particles whose interactions are weighted by a smoothing kernel, and its accuracy rests on a property the equations never enforce explicitly: that each particle's neighbourhood is spatially balanced. On a disordered distribution the discrete kernel-gradient sum Σj∇WijVj — identically zero on a symmetric arrangement — acquires large residuals, and states that violate minimum particle spacing cannot be used to start or restart a simulation. Classical remedies (particle shifting, transport-velocity formulations, packing algorithms; §2) repair this inside the solver loop, iteratively and at every step.

We ask whether the repair can be learned once and applied as a standalone operator. The question is sharper than it looks: a corrector of this kind trained only on the spacing constraint — the natural first attempt, and our own predecessor model — produces clouds that satisfy the constraint while quadrupling the kernel-gradient residual (1.278 against 0.326 uncorrected), making its outputs useless as restart states. Fixing the geometry is not the same as fixing the physics.

This paper shows that a compact message-passing network can do both, provided the physics enters twice: as a kernel-gradient residual in the loss, and as a fixed SPH-kernel-shaped weighting in the architecture. Our contributions:

  • A deployable physics-informed corrector. Trained on 49-particle synthetic lattices, it corrects a real 2,500-particle SPH trajectory to mean |KG| 0.127 — 2.2× better than the Transport Velocity baseline — at 0.19 s per state on CPU, validated by an actual SPH re-simulation, and transfers unchanged to a bounded obstacle scene at 11.7× coordinate scale (§4.2).
  • The physics term is an optimisation enabler, not a regulariser. Ablating it does not merely degrade quality: training diverges, and the deployed model reproduces the predecessor's failure (|KG| 1.471). Neither the constraint terms nor the physics term function alone (§4.3).
  • Small-N benchmarks misrank architectures against deployment. Two parameter-matched competitors beat our model on the training-scale benchmark and lose on the real task (§4.4); single-mechanism ablations locate what transfers — the fixed kernel weighting with additive aggregation (§4.5).
  • Deployment guidance with measured uncertainty. An operating-point sweep, a degenerate mode invisible to the task metrics, and a claim audit against measured seed variance (§4.6–4.8, appendix).

2Related work

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Flag: keep — sized for ~0.5 page. Citation keys refer to paper/references.bib (15 entries, venues verified 2026-08-10); replace with your \cite{} commands. Full positioning notes: paper/RELATED_WORK.md.

Particle regularity in SPH. SPH accuracy degrades on disordered particle distributions, and a family of classical remedies exists: particle shifting moves particles down concentration gradients [xu2009accuracy, lind2012incompressible], the transport-velocity formulation regularises positions inside the momentum equation [adami2013transport], and packing algorithms iterate a damped dynamics to prepare initial conditions [colagrossi2012particle, diehl2015generating]. All of these are solver-coupled: they run as iterative physics loops inside, or ahead of, the simulation. Our corrector addresses the same defect — a distribution violating minimum spacing (equivalently, a blue-noise condition [bridson2007fast]) with asymmetric kernel-gradient sums [morris1997modeling] — but as a learned, standalone operator applied to arbitrary states with no solver in the loop.

Learned particle simulation. Graph-network simulators [sanchezgonzalez2020learning, pfaff2021learning] learn dynamics rollouts over particle or mesh states. Neural SPH [toshev2024neural] shows that such rollouts suffer tensile-instability-like particle clustering and repairs them by inserting SPH relaxation steps at inference; diffSPH [winchenbach2025diffsph] casts shifting itself as an optimisation over differentiable SPH operators. Our work sits between these: rather than adding physics relaxation to a learned simulator, we learn the relaxation itself — and our architecture is precisely a GNS-class network with its learned edge weighting replaced by the fixed SPH kernel it would otherwise have to approximate (§4.5).

Physics-informed losses. Embedding physical residuals in training objectives is standard since PINNs [raissi2019physics]. Our kernel-gradient term belongs to this family, but our ablation sharpens the usual claim: the term is not a soft constraint that improves accuracy — without it, training diverges and the corrector reproduces the failure mode of its predecessor (§4.3). The physics is an optimisation enabler.

Point-cloud architectures. PointNet and its hierarchical and graph-based successors [qi2017pointnet, qi2017pointnetpp, wang2019dynamic] are the standard learned operators on unordered point sets. We use them as parameter-matched baselines and find their generic inductive biases — global pooling, feature-space graphs, max aggregation — fail this task (§4.4), and that small-N benchmark rankings of them invert at deployment scale.

Finally, while we instantiate the recipe for SPH, nothing in it is SPH-specific: the objective pairs a minimum-spacing constraint with the target method's own consistency residual, and the architecture builds the corresponding interaction kernel into its message weighting. Substituting the residual — e.g. an energy-based term for molecular-dynamics initial conditions, in place of the kernel-gradient term — yields a corrector for other particle methods; we return to this in the outlook.

Reviewer-facing positioning (keep in mind, not in the paper): Neural SPH keeps the learned simulator and adds classical relaxation; we learn the relaxation. If asked “why not just run classical relaxation?” — the deployment table answers it: Transport Velocity reaches 0.274, the learned corrector 0.127.

3Method

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Flag: keep, ≈0.9 page with one equation block. If your Methods section also covers the objective, move the loss equation from §4.1 here.

Corrector network. The corrector is an L-round message-passing network over the radius graph of the cloud. Node states start at zero, so all signal enters through pairwise geometry; one round computes, for every ordered pair within the cutoff radius rc,

eij(l) = MLPe(l) [hi, hj, xi−xj, dij, relu(rd−dij)],   hi ← hi + MLPn(l) Σj wij eij(l),   wij = (1−(dij/rc)²)² / Σk(·) after L rounds, Δxi = tanh(MLPo(hi)) · 1.2 rd. All relative positions use the minimum image on periodic domains.

Two design choices carry the results. First, the message weight wij is a fixed, SPH-kernel-shaped function of distance, not learned attention: it is smooth, compactly supported (identically zero at d ≥ rc), and scale-free once coordinates are normalised by rd. Every near pair contributes — violating or not — which is what makes the kernel-gradient signal visible; overlap depth remains explicit through the relu(rd−d) feature. §4.5 shows this weighting, together with additive aggregation, is precisely the component that survives the transfer from training to deployment scale. Second, the receptive field is matched to the physics: with rc = 2Δx (the SPH smoothing length h) and L=4 rounds, information propagates ≈8 particle spacings — covering the quintic kernel's support of 6Δx — so kernel-gradient symmetry is learnable as a local property, which is what permits size generalisation. The network is translation-invariant by construction (it sees only relative positions) but deliberately not rotation-equivariant, matching a fixed simulation frame.

Whole-cloud deployment. Training uses dense N×N interactions at small N; deployment runs the identical weights over an explicit edge list (exact, since wij vanishes beyond rc). One correction pass scales the cloud by rdtrain/rdtest into the training geometry, builds the periodic edge list with a cell-indexed neighbour search, applies one forward pass, and unscales; the corrector is applied for k such passes. Solid boundaries are represented by ghost particles filling the obstacle interior at spacing rd, concatenated before each pass and re-pinned after it, so the solid never drifts (§4.2).

4.1Setup

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Task. Given a 2-D point cloud x ∈ ℝN×2 on a periodic domain that violates a minimum pairwise distance rd, predict per-point displacements Δx such that x+Δx satisfies the constraint and is usable as a restart state for an SPH simulation. Restart quality is measured by the discrete SPH consistency condition

KGi = Σj ∇W(rij, h) Vj  →  0 W: quintic spline, h = 2Δx; KGi vanishes on a symmetric neighbourhood, and mean |KGi| is our primary metric (lower is better).

Training data. Clouds are generated online per batch on the unit torus: a randomly translated 7×7 lattice (N=49, spacing 1/7, rd = 0.14 ≈ 0.98·spacing) with bounded jitter, perturbed by Gaussian noise of amplitude drawn from [0, σ·rd] with σ=0.6 (standard) or σ=1.0 (hard). All geometry is minimum-image periodic.

Loss. All models are trained with the same physics-informed objective

L = λ1 mean relu(rd−dij)  +  λ2 mean |Δx|  +  λ3 meani |KGi|² λ1=1/rd=7.14,  λ2=0.1 λ1/(N−1)=0.0149,  λ3=0.27. The KG term is soft and training-only — never enforced at inference.

Protocol. Every architecture shares one recipe: AdamW (lr 10−3, wd 10−4), cosine schedule over 104 iterations, batch 32, K=5 unrolled correction passes with per-step detachment, and an identical bounded output head tanh(·)×1.2 rd. Parameter counts are matched to 350 k ±0.8%. No per-architecture hyperparameter search is performed (discussed in §4.8). Because training can degenerate initialisation-dependently (§4.7), any degeneration claim requires ≥3 seeds.

Evaluation. One scorer evaluates every arm: periodic metrics on 64 fixed held-out clouds (synthetic regime), and on a real N=2500 SPH trajectory (1002 timesteps; disordered regime t ≥ 300) through a whole-cloud sparse corrector with coordinate scaling rdtrain/rdtest. Sparse and dense forward passes agree to 4×10−7 (18 checks across all architectures). Corrected states from the production configuration were additionally validated by an actual SPH re-simulation. Measurement spread over three identical-recipe runs is σ≈9% on synthetic |KG| but only 3.5% on trajectory |KG| (deployment averages over 2500 particles × 15 timesteps); differences below these thresholds are not claimed. Deployment costs 0.189 s/timestep on CPU and 0.049 s on GPU at N=2500, k=5.

4.2Correction of a real SPH trajectory

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Table 1 reports deployment on the held-out trajectory. The corrector reduces mean |KG| from 0.326 to 0.127 — 2.6× below the uncorrected state and 2.2× below Transport Velocity, the classical particle-shifting baseline — while raising mean neighbour spacing to 0.0195 (rdtest=0.02) and reducing the spread of that spacing (nn CV) from 18.7% to 2.8%, i.e. a visibly regular near-lattice arrangement (Fig. 1). Prior work without the symmetry term (model9) quadruples |KG| instead; we return to this in §4.3.

Generality: a bounded scene with an obstacle

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Flag: keep — six lines plus a small table, and it is the answer to the single-scenario objection.

To test transfer beyond the periodic trajectory we deploy the same production checkpoint, without retraining or retuning, on a qualitatively different scenario: initialising 6,100 particles around a gear-shaped obstacle in a bounded, non-periodic domain at rd=0.012 (coordinate scale 11.7× the training rd, versus 7.0× on the trajectory), with the obstacle interior filled by 832 fixed ghost particles re-pinned at every pass. The kernel-gradient metric is not defined here (it presumes a periodic domain), so we report the structural metrics. The corrector produces the same signature as on the trajectory — near-uniform spacing (nn CV 3.0% versus 2.8%), local rather than bulk motion (drift 5.8%), and comparable neighbourhood rewiring (knn-keep 0.64) — despite the different topology, boundary conditions, density, and 2.4× larger cloud.

4.3Loss ablation: the physics term is an optimisation enabler

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Table 3 ablates each term of the objective. Removing the KG term (λ3=0) does not merely degrade quality — it reproduces the failure mode of prior work. Deployed on the trajectory, the ablated model yields |KG| 1.471, 4.4× worse than applying no correction at all, and adjacent to model9 (1.278), the predecessor whose corrected clouds were unusable as restarts and whose failure motivated this work. The ablation puts the breakage back.

λ3=0 (physics term removed)17.6%0.14070.7011.4714/4 degen.
λ1=λ2=0 (symmetry only)−19.5%0.39480.1323.0091
λ2=0 (no displacement reg.)0.0%0.22601.000—1 (degen.)

Table 3: Loss ablation. All cells trained with the shared recipe and scored identically; trajectory column as in Table 1. knn-keep is the mean Jaccard overlap of each particle's 6-NN set before/after correction. The λ3=0 arm degenerates in 4 of 4 initialisations; the symmetry-only arm destroys the arrangement it is given (knn-keep 0.132). Neither objective functions alone.

Three independent signals support the λ3 result. First, removing the symmetry term costs 65 points of violation reduction — the term it was supposedly only regularising. Second, training diverges without it: deterministic validation loss reaches its minimum at iteration 500 of 10,000 and never improves, whereas the full objective improves monotonically to the final iterate. Third, the final iterate degenerates into a saturated uniform translation (§4.7). We attribute this to gradient density: the violation term is a mean over N² pairs of which only O(N) violate, so its gradient dilutes as easy violations clear, while the KG term supplies a dense per-particle gradient throughout training.

Two architectures beat ours on this benchmark: GNS at high disorder (0.0205 vs 0.0308) and the max-aggregation variant of §4.5 (0.0106, 2× better). Both lose on the real task (Fig. 2): at N=2500, GNS reaches only 0.132–0.143 (three runs, no overlap with ours at 0.123–0.127), and under the matched production training regime it reaches 0.242 — barely better than Transport Velocity. Model selection on the small-N benchmark alone would therefore have shipped the worse deployer, twice.

4.5What transfers: fixed kernel and additive aggregation

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Flag: keep the claim, the table, and the closing argument; the rung descriptions can compress to one sentence each.

To locate the mechanism behind the benchmark–deployment reversal we ablate model12 one component at a time, in a variant whose baseline configuration is bit-identical to the production model. Two single-mechanism rungs are decisive: nokernel replaces the fixed proximity kernel (1−(d/rc)²)² with a learned scalar gate, changing nothing else; wmax keeps the kernel but replaces the weighted mean with a weighted max, changing nothing else.

Table 5: Mechanism ablation, grouped by whether the fixed geometric kernel is applied to messages and aggregation is additive. Ranges are over available runs (1–3 per variant). The groups do not overlap at deployment: 0.118–0.127 versus 0.132–0.170 across eleven runs, four architectures, and three aggregation schemes.

Changing either component alone — and nothing else — moves the model out of the good group. This matches the structure of the objective: |KG| is a weighted sum of kernel gradients, so an architecture that must drive it to zero at a cardinality it never saw needs both the distance weighting (scale-free by construction) and the summation. A learned weighting fits the training cardinality's statistics; a max discards the balance information that summation carries. Per-particle normalisation, by contrast, is not required — removing it (nonorm) transfers marginally better than the production model.

4.6Operating point and training cardinality

KEEP — MAIN BODYCUT IF TIGHT

Flag: keep the k=1 warning, the k=8 trade-off sentence, and the N=100 result in the main body (~half a page with Table 6); the k-curve figure can move to the appendix.

The corrector is applied iteratively; Table 6 sweeps the number of passes k on the trajectory. Three facts matter for deployment. A single pass is harmful: k=1 yields |KG| 0.466 against 0.333 uncorrected, and the corrector only becomes a net win from k ≥ 3. |KG| then decreases monotonically with no floor through k=40 (0.068). The violation–symmetry trade-off instead appears in the constraint metric: illegal pairs reach their minimum at k=8 and rise thereafter — beyond that point, additional symmetry is bought at legality's expense. We use k=5 (sim-validated) for all validated claims and recommend k=8 as the best all-round operating point.

Training cardinality has a larger effect than any architectural choice we tested: retraining the identical architecture at N=100 (with λ3 ∝ 1/N² rescaled accordingly, appendix Table A2) improves deployment |KG| by 31% to 0.087 — the best result in this work — consistent with reducing the gap between training and deployment scale (receptive field 1.14 of the box at N=49 versus 0.80 at N=100, against 0.16 at deployment). This checkpoint is a single run and has not been re-simulated.

4.7A failure mode invisible to the task metrics

MOVE TO APPENDIX

Flag: move the figure and most of the prose to the appendix; keep the two bolded sentences in the main body (they justify the seeding protocol and the bulk-drift diagnostic).

Roughly half of training runs for several variants degenerate into a saturated uniform translation: every particle moves by the same vector at exactly the output bound. Because every term of the objective depends only on relative positions, this state is invisible to |KG| and illegal% — both report the cloud unchanged while it translates a full domain length over five passes (Fig. 3). It is a tanh-saturation trap: once the output head saturates, its gradient vanishes and no signal recovers it. Whether a run falls in depends only on initialisation (e.g. DGCNN at σ=1.0: 2 of 4 seeds), so we (i) log the bulk-drift fraction |mean Δx|/mean|Δx| at every evaluation, and (ii) accept degeneration claims only at 3/3 seeds — a bar only the λ3=0 arm meets (4/4).

Figure 3 (appendix): Displacement decomposed into bulk translation + local restructuring, one pass, identical cloud. Working models are 3–9% bulk; PointNet's local component is empty (10−4) — its entire output is the translation, which the task metrics cannot see.

4.8Limitations

KEEP — MAIN BODY
  • One trajectory, one solver validation. The KG results derive from a single 2-D SPH run. The bounded obstacle scene (§4.2) shows the structural signature transfers to a second scenario, but it has no KG measure and no solver validation of its own.
  • Shared hyperparameters favour our model. The common recipe (λ3, schedule, learning rate) was originally tuned on model12; equal-budget comparison without per-architecture search is the stated protocol, but the asymmetry is real.
  • Best ≠ validated. The re-simulation was performed with the production N=49 checkpoint at k=5; the stronger N=100 and k ≥ 8 operating points are measured, not solver-validated, and the N=100 result is a single run.
  • Scale limits of the loss. The minimum-image KG term is exact only for N > ~50 on the unit torus (appendix Table A2); small-N ablations are not meaningful under this objective. 3-D requires a 3-D kernel and is future work.

5Conclusion and outlook

KEEP — MAIN BODY

Flag: draft prose, ≈0.4 page.

We presented a learned corrector that turns constraint-violating particle distributions into usable SPH restart states, validated end-to-end by re-simulation. Its two load-bearing ingredients are the same piece of physics entering twice: the kernel-gradient residual in the objective — without which training itself diverges and the corrector reproduces the failure of constraint-only prior work — and the fixed, scale-free SPH kernel in the message weighting, which single-mechanism ablations identify (together with additive aggregation) as the component that carries a model trained on 49 particles to a 2,500-particle deployment. Along the way we found that the small-scale synthetic benchmark inverts architecture rankings relative to the real task, twice; we suggest treating deployment-scale evaluation as mandatory for learned particle operators.

Outlook. Four directions follow directly. First, validation of the stronger operating points found here — k=8 passes and training at N=100 (31% better |KG| than the validated configuration) — by re-simulation. Second, three dimensions: the corrector and its sparse deployment path are dimension-generic, and only the quintic kernel-gradient primitive needs a 3-D normalisation. Third, disorder: the noise level acts as a physical temperature, and the corrector's behaviour across it is uncharted. Fourth, other particle methods: the recipe — a spacing constraint plus the target method's own consistency residual, with the corresponding kernel built into the architecture — is not SPH-specific; molecular-dynamics initial conditions with an energy-based residual are the natural next instantiation.
